title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind
summary: Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. They're too good at describing the work The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb. It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention. I think I've found a low-effort way to do this that feels right. Hide most of it in a details/summary The HTML elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this: < details > < summary > Claude Opus 5.5 < h2 > The hook Plugins implement < code > register_agent_reference_types(datasette) ... When rendered, it looks like this : Crucially, is supported in GitHub Markdown . You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display just the summary plus an expansion arrow. title: Advice on keeping a job
summary: Hey all, so, I have been doing this for about 6 years now on a legacy on-prem stack. Every time I try to transition to something more modern - dlt/dbt I get shot down. Stick to .NET, that's what the company wants. I try to introduce metadata importing, and no time for that, just stick to what you have. Well, I finally got what I want. We're moving to the cloud. Only it's been decided we don't have enough python/pyspark background, so someone else is writing an engine for us. I have been told I am going from owning the entire pipeline to only owning bronze/silver and the BAs will own gold. And Bronze/Silver will be automated. The best I get is to tweak some yaml files. Anything related to actual code will be handled by the "developers". I can see this maybe lasting 6 months to a year, until all of our sources are in yaml form and there's nothing left for my team of 3 people to do. To be honest, most of this is exactly what I wanted - except I was hoping I would get to retain ownership of the gold, and possibly have some idea of what my job looked like still. Any ideas from anyone who has faced similar, being automated out and any advice on how you keep seeing yourself having value and a job? submitted by /u/-crucible- [link] [comments]

title: 5 big Windows headaches and how to fix them
summary: Windows has come a long way since its initial release in 1985. From its birth, it gained a reputation as a kludge of an operating system, ugly and unloved, something that would get the job done (mostly) but cause lots of unpleasantness along the way. Who can forget struggling to do something as simple as install a new printer? Or the dreaded Blue Screen of Death that would pop up for no apparent reason and crash Windows, taking all your work along with it? The worst of those days are long behind us. Over time, Microsoft managed to kill many of the gremlins that bedeviled the operating system. Windows 11 is quite stable, and not nearly as confusing and cumbersome as previous versions. That’s not to say all is well with Windows, though. There’s plenty that still goes wrong and plenty of design choices that can trip you up when you’re just trying to work. Don’t fear. Help is on the way. Here are five of the worst things about Windows — and how to make them better so you can get some real work done. 1. Windows slows down with age It seems inevitable: You buy a new PC and it runs like greased lightning. Then several years later, it’s slow as molasses. PCs, just like people, slow down with age. But there’s a lot you can do to speed up a years-old PC and make it zippy again. First, disable programs that run at startup unnecessarily. As you install new software, or when existing software gets updated, it’s not uncommon that an increasing number of apps and processes run at startup when you don’t really need them. To fix that, first launch Task Manager in one of these ways: Press Ctrl-Shift-Esc. Right-click the taskbar and select Task Manager . Type task manager into the Windows search box and select it from the results. Click the Startup apps icon in the left-hand navigation pane — it’s the speedometer icon, fifth from the top. title: Getting ready for Apple’s next big thing: MacBook Neo 2
summary: Apple is on track to sell eight million MacBook Neo systems by the end of the year, and it expects the next generation of the device to do even better when it arrives in spring. To achieve this, Apple needs to remain focused on what made the product such a success . There is no doubt it has been a success. At one point Apple was complaining that it was unable to churn these things out fast enough . Tom Boger, Apple’s Vice President of Mac and iPad Product Marketing, recently called the introduction of the MacBook Neo “ a huge momentum creator ,” adding, “We’re bringing more new-to-Mac customers than we ever have in the 42 years that the Mac has been around.” He called this “remarkable” for a product that has been around for so long. A hit in the hard ground It’s also remarkable given the current environment. Consumer electronic sales are taking a beating from the combined effects of war, political instability, and AI-flation. As prices climb, cash-strapped buyers, both consumer and IT purchasers, have become much more discerning when hunting for the best available deal. Apple seems to be thriving all the same. Even at its higher-than-launch price (the $599 MacBook Neo now costs $699), Neo has stayed in the top three laptops sold on Amazon US since launch. All three of Amazon’s top selling laptops are Macs at time of writing. While global PC sales fell 21%, Apple’s global market share reached almost 10% . One data point claims that the Neo grabbed 23% of Apple’s total notebook sales volume within just 21 days of its release, purloining market share from midrange Windows devices and Chromebooks. Where the MacBook Neo won Where has it excelled? Consumers have flocked to it, but it has seen particular success in the education and enterprise markets. title: The Guardian view on Jensen Huang’s affair: why did Trump ignore the warnings? | Editorial
summary: The AI chip boss’s actions raise urgent questions about corporate influence, national security and the US president’s willingness to listen to intelligence warnings It could be the plot of a spy thriller. One of the most powerful figures in the AI revolution admitted to having an affair with a Chinese businesswomen said to have passed intelligence to Beijing. When Donald Trump was briefed about the Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang’s liaisons with Alice Huang, he took no action. Perhaps he thought only marriage vows had been broken. Or perhaps Mr Trump was willing to overlook the conduct of a friend who championed his unpopular datacentre expansion, whose company donated to his White House ballroom and who echoed his opposition to AI safeguards against expert advice. Nvidia became the cornerstone of AI by supplying brute computing power. As tech giants scrambled for the firm’s graphics processing units (GPUs), Mr Huang sold the picks and shovels for the AI gold rush – and amassed a $160bn fortune. When China joined the race for tech supremacy, Nvidia’s microchips became a national security issue. In October 2022, the US slapped export controls on GPU sales to China. Thirty months later, Nvidia was effectively banned from selling to Beijing. Mr Huang lobbied for looser controls. Such was his sway with Mr Trump that the White House scrapped Biden-era global AI chip restrictions and then permitted sales of Nvidia’s prized H200 processors to Chinese customers. title: How neurosymbolic AI can transform enterprise decision-making
summary: Agentic AI has become a powerful enterprise business tool with increasing capabilities, and it has never been easier to address business pain points by applying a large language model (LLM) to develop a plausible automated solution. But is that solution as reliable as you need it to be, especially when the insights gleaned are used to inform critical business decisions? LLMs are incredible resources that play a significant role in a business’s agentic AI infrastructure. But when they have to work across complex data sets, business policies, industry regulations, decision hierarchies, and multiple software systems, they do not inherently provide the enterprise-grade provenance needed to show which evidence, assumptions, constraints, and decision logic produced a recommendation. Additionally, when gathering inputs from a volume of data sources, the accuracy of their outputs can break down and potentially create hallucinations. If business decisions are made based on LLM outputs that can’t be explained or may be inaccurate, it can create significant consequences that impact product sales, revenue, compliance, or customers. The problem is that the LLM is asked to carry too much of the enterprise reasoning without the harness and enterprise foundation around it. A structured foundation for decision-making While enterprise interest in agentic AI has grown substantially over the past few years, what works in concept hasn’t always proven results in the pilot phase and beyond. A common reason agentic AI pilots can fail in production is that an LLM is asked to carry too much of the enterprise reasoning without the support of an enterprise foundation. LLMs are powerful for some use cases, like demos, but enterprise decision-making will always require structure beyond a good prompt. title: How components can help us govern agents
summary: My most-cited BYTE cover story was 1994’s Componentware , which made the case for a two-tier architecture best exemplified then by Visual Basic and its component ecosystem. The prevailing strategy for software reuse, object-oriented programming , hadn’t gained the traction we all expected. Visual Basic showed us why it hadn’t. Objects were written in the same languages, and by the same specialized coders, as the programs that reused those objects. VB flipped the script. Code-savvy component builders created building blocks that domain-savvy systems thinkers could wire together. Then the web flipped the script again. The browser was the new canvas, and it left the component ecosystem behind. Plugins came and went. The web platform eventually did define standards for components but they’ve been eclipsed by the web’s de facto standard framework, React , and its component architecture. And just like objects 30 years ago, React components are both produced and consumed by specialized coders. There wasn’t a good way for a modern solution builder to tap into React’s component ecosystem. The framework that I co-maintain, XMLUI , harks back to the VB model. A UI is defined by concise semantic XML markup that refers to a catalog of components . There is no visual canvas but, as we debated whether or how to recreate that experience, the question became moot. When agents write declarative markup in conversation with us, direct manipulation matters less than it used to. A better target language for LLMs It’s no accident that Markdown has become a primary way for humans and AIs to collaborate. Why not HTML and CSS? Markdown constrains AIs to a smaller set of patterns, and that’s a good general rule. Our new agentic team members are powerful but undisciplined. Left to their own devices they behave in unpredictable ways. The fewer degrees of freedom we allow them, the better things will go for all of us. The same principle applies to coding.
